title: YOU FOLLOWED THEM FOR THEIR CONTENT. BUT WHAT IF JESUS ASKED WHY?
paragraphs:
YOU FOLLOWED THEM FOR THEIR CONTENT. BUT WHAT IF JESUS ASKED WHY?
Is Following Adult Creators on Social Media a Form of Compromise—or Can a Christian Really Say, “I’m Just Looking”?
There is a kind of compromise that does not feel like compromise anymore.
It does not begin in a motel room.
It does not begin with an affair.
Sometimes it begins with a blue button that says Follow.
One tap.
That’s all.
Nobody at church knows.
Your spouse may never notice.
Your parents cannot see it.
Your Christian friends probably will not ask.
And because you have not physically touched anyone, messaged anyone, or perhaps even purchased anything, you tell yourself the easiest sentence in the world to believe:
“I’m only following them.”
But there is another question.
One that reaches much deeper than whether you technically committed a physical sexual act.
Why are you following them?
That question changes everything.
Because Jesus has always been interested in the place beneath the behavior.
The heart.
And if you stay with me until the end, we are going somewhere uncomfortable—but not toward condemnation.
Toward a cross.
Toward grace.
Toward the possibility that the thing you are afraid Jesus will expose may be the very thing He wants to free you from.
Maybe you follow an adult creator because you find that person attractive.
Maybe you tell yourself it is harmless because the content on your feed is not technically explicit.
Maybe you follow models, influencers, actors, adult entertainers, thirst-trap accounts, or creators whose entire online presence is deliberately sexualized.
Maybe you never comment.
Never message.
You just watch.
Scroll.
Return.
Watch again.
And somewhere along the way, your conscience became quieter.
Not necessarily because the behavior became holier.
Maybe because it became familiar.
That distinction matters.
The Bible does not contain a verse saying, “Thou shalt not follow an adult creator on social media.”
So we must be careful.
We should never manufacture commandments God did not give.
But neither should we use technological novelty to escape moral principles God made unmistakably clear.
The real biblical question is not simply:
“Is following this account forbidden?”
The deeper question is:
“What am I deliberately placing before my eyes, what am I inviting into my desires, and where is it leading my heart?”
Thousands of years before smartphones, Job said something astonishing:
בְּרִית כָּרַתִּי לְעֵינָי
Berit karati le'enai.
“I have made a covenant with my eyes.”
That is the force of Job 31:1.
The Hebrew בְּרִית — berit means covenant.
Job was describing intentionality.
Not accidental sight.
Not the involuntary recognition that another human being is attractive.
Not merely existing in a world where sexuality is visible.
He was talking about governing what he allowed his eyes to become attached to.
That matters enormously because Christianity does not teach that noticing beauty is sin.
Being sexually attracted is not automatically sin.
Temptation itself is not identical to sin; Jesus Himself was tempted, yet without sin.

And seeing provocative content unexpectedly while scrolling is not morally identical to deliberately searching for it, following it, revisiting it, lingering over it, or using another person's body as fuel for lust.
That distinction may rescue someone reading this from unnecessary shame.
But it may also remove somebody else's favorite excuse.
Because there is a difference between something appearing before your eyes...
and arranging your digital life so that it keeps coming back.
A follow is not merely observation.
In ordinary social-media use, following usually communicates something like:
Show me more of this.
Put this person in my feed.
Bring this content back tomorrow.
Keep the connection available.
And if the reason you want that recurring access is sexual stimulation, fantasy, lust, or the enjoyment of someone else's sexualized body, then the issue is no longer merely technological.
It has become spiritual.
Jesus went directly there.
In Matthew 5:28, the Greek text reads in part:
πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn...
The crucial idea is not merely that someone happened to see a woman.
Jesus speaks of looking πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι—looking with the purpose or movement toward lustful desire.
He concludes that such a person has already committed adultery with her ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ—“in his heart.”
Read that carefully.
Jesus did not condemn eyesight.
He confronted intentional lust.
That means the Christian question cannot stop at:
“Did I touch anyone?”
Jesus takes us deeper:
“What was I doing with them in my heart?”
And suddenly that harmless follow button becomes harder to hide behind.
Because if you follow someone specifically because their body sexually excites you...
if you wait for provocative posts...
if you revisit their profile when you are lonely...
if their pictures become material for fantasy...
if you would immediately become uncomfortable if Jesus physically sat beside you while you scrolled...
then perhaps the question is no longer whether this is “technically pornography.”
Perhaps the question is whether you are feeding something Christ told you not to feed.
And before anyone weaponizes this article against somebody else, hear this clearly.
This applies to men and women.
It applies to married people and single people.
It applies to pastors and teenagers, ministry workers and new believers.
It applies whether the person being lusted after is female or male.
And this article is not permission to degrade adult creators themselves.
They are not objects.
They are human beings.
Image-bearers.
People with histories, wounds, choices, families, fears, sins, hopes, and souls.
Christians must never fight objectification by dehumanizing the person being objectified.
Jesus died for sinners.
That includes sexual sinners.
That includes consumers.
That includes creators.
That includes you.
That includes me.
The Gospel gives nobody permission to stand at the foot of the cross and boast.
But grace also does not require us to rename compromise as freedom.
Paul wrote:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
That is 1 Corinthians 6:18.
Notice the verb.
Φεύγετε — pheugete.
Flee.
Paul does not say negotiate with it.
Study how close you can stand to it.
Follow it but promise yourself not to go further.
Keep it available because you have “self-control.”
Ask how much sexual stimulation you can consume before God technically calls it sin.
Flee.
Sometimes spiritual maturity looks surprisingly unimpressive.
Sometimes it looks like an unfollow.
A block.
A deleted bookmark.
A conversation with your spouse.
A confession to someone trustworthy.
A phone left outside the bedroom.
A filter installed when nobody forced you to install it.
Sometimes holiness looks like losing access to something your flesh desperately wanted to keep.
And perhaps that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because some people reading this are not really asking whether following adult creators is compromise.
You already know why you follow them.
You are actually asking:
“How much can I keep without feeling like I have walked away from Jesus?”
That is a different question.
And it is the question compromise loves.
Compromise rarely walks through the front door announcing:
“I am here to destroy your intimacy with Christ.”
It whispers:
It isn't that serious.
Everyone does it.
At least you're not sleeping with anybody.
You're still going to church.
You're still praying.
You're still married.
You aren't buying the explicit stuff.
You're just looking.
Just looking.
Those two words have protected a lot of hidden rooms.
Then nighttime comes.
The house becomes quiet.
Your thumb moves almost automatically.
One profile.
Another.
Another.
You feel the rush.
Then afterward...
silence.
Maybe shame.
Maybe numbness.
Maybe nothing anymore.
And that “nothing” can be more frightening than the shame.
Because at least shame sometimes tells you your conscience is still fighting.
There are people who once felt convicted after five minutes and now can scroll sexualized content for an hour without feeling much at all.
Not every feeling of guilt comes from God, and Christians must never confuse obsessive shame with holiness.
But neither should we celebrate a conscience simply because it has learned to stop protesting.

Paul gives believers another filter in Philippians 4:8: whatever is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, commendable, excellent, and worthy of praise—these are the things upon which the Christian mind is called to dwell.
That does not mean Christians must live terrified of every beautiful person or every swimsuit photograph.
It means discipleship reaches the imagination.
Your attention matters.
Your mental diet matters.
What you repeatedly rehearse matters.
What you deliberately place before your eyes matters.
And here is a question worth sitting with:
Is this account helping me see this person as someone made in God's image—or training me to consume that person's body?
Do not answer quickly.
Especially if you are married.
Because there may be another human being sleeping beside you who cannot compete with a digitally curated parade of bodies.
They were never supposed to.
Your spouse has morning breath.
Bad days.
Wrinkles eventually.
Stress.
Ordinary clothes.
Illness.
Exhaustion.
A real body that changes.
A real personality that sometimes irritates you.
A real soul requiring patience and sacrifice.
The screen asks almost nothing from you.
It presents selected images, controlled lighting, flattering angles, editing, fantasy, novelty.
And then you may unknowingly bring that artificial marketplace of attention into a covenant where another human being is trying to be loved.
That can become devastating.
Not because your spouse must be the only attractive person you ever notice.
Scripture never commands pretending attractive people cease to exist after marriage.
But covenant love teaches the heart not to turn every attraction into consumption.
There is a difference.
A profound one.
Maybe you are single.
Then hear this too.
Purity is not something you practice merely so that one day you can give a future spouse an impressive résumé.
Purity belongs first to Christ.
Your body belongs to Christ.
Your mind belongs to Christ.
Your sexuality belongs under the lordship of Christ.

Paul's argument immediately surrounding his command to flee sexual immorality is breathtaking: the believer's body is for the Lord, united to Christ, indwelt by the Holy Spirit, bought with a price, and therefore called to glorify God.
That means biblical sexual ethics are not ultimately:
“God hates sex.”
Quite the opposite.
God created sexuality.
The Christian story does not call the body dirty.
It calls the body significant.
So significant that Paul says:
You were bought with a price.
Therefore glorify God in your body.
And there is the deeper issue.
Not merely:
“Can I follow this creator?”
But:
“Can I glorify Christ in why I am following this creator?”
That question reaches places legalism cannot.

Suppose you follow an adult creator because that individual also discusses business, fitness, culture, or another legitimate subject, and you have no sexual motive, do not consume explicit material, and are not being drawn toward lust.
Scripture does not give us grounds to declare the mere digital act of following that person intrinsically sinful in every conceivable circumstance.
We should be biblically precise.
The identity or occupation of the account owner does not magically make every click sinful.

But if following that account repeatedly draws you into lust, sexual fantasy, explicit material, temptation, secrecy, masturbation fueled by that person's content, dishonesty toward your spouse, or a pattern you know weakens your obedience to Christ, then arguing over whether the follow itself is technically sinful may be missing the entire point.
Paul writes elsewhere that not everything permissible is beneficial and that he will not be mastered by anything.
There are things you may be capable of touching without technically violating a command that nevertheless begin to master you.
And Christians were not redeemed merely to ask:
“What can I get away with?”
We were redeemed to ask:
“How can Christ be glorified in me?”
There is another uncomfortable dimension.
Your follow is attention.
Attention has value.
Online, attention can become reach, influence, social proof, and sometimes money.
That does not mean every follow makes you morally responsible for everything another person does, nor can we simplistically claim that clicking “follow” equals directly financing pornography.
That would overstate the case.
But Christians should still ask whether their attention is helping sustain a digital ecosystem they privately believe is destructive.
You cannot control the internet.
You can decide what you intentionally reward with your eyes.
Yet this is where I refuse to leave you drowning in guilt.
Because perhaps you have already gone much further than following.
Maybe you have watched pornography for years.
Maybe you have paid creators.
Maybe you have hidden transactions.
Maybe you have lied to your husband.
Maybe you have lied to your wife.
Maybe you are the creator.
Maybe sexual attention became the way you learned to feel valuable.
Maybe pornography became anesthesia for loneliness.
Maybe fantasy became the place you went whenever real life hurt.
Maybe you have promised God fifty times:
“This is the last time.”
And then came fifty-one.
And now you are reading an article about social media when underneath the question is something much more desperate:
“Would Jesus still want me if He knew everything?”
He knows.
Everything.
And the Gospel is still the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come for people who had successfully hidden their scandal.
He came for sinners.
The cross is not God's reward for people who cleaned themselves before arriving.
The cross is where guilty people discover what grace actually costs.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ calls sinners to repentance and faith.
And repentance is not God saying:
“Become clean enough so I can finally love you.”
Repentance is the turning of a sinner who has finally realized that the thing he was clutching cannot save him—and Christ can.
Grace does not whisper:
Keep the chains.
Grace unlocks them.
Grace does not say:
Your sin doesn't matter.
Grace says:
Your sin mattered enough for Christ to bleed, and His mercy is greater than the thing you thought could never be forgiven.
This is why Christian conviction and Christian condemnation must never be confused.
Conviction brings the hidden thing toward Christ.
Condemnation tells you to hide from Him.
Conviction says:
“Come into the light.”
Condemnation says:
“If anyone knew, you would be finished.”
The Gospel says:
Jesus already knows—and He is calling you out of darkness.
Maybe tonight your repentance begins with something almost laughably small.
Unfollow.
Unfollow.
Unfollow.
Delete.
Block.
Cancel.
Then stop pretending the battle ends there.
Bring somebody trustworthy into the fight.
If you are trapped in a compulsive pattern, seek mature pastoral accountability and, where appropriate, qualified professional help.
If you betrayed your spouse, do not use “grace” as another hiding place.
Walk toward truth, wisdom, repentance, and restoration.
If you stumble again, do not turn a fall into an identity.
Run back to Christ.
Confess.
Get up.
Fight again.
Sanctification is not pretending temptation disappeared.
It is learning where to run when temptation appears.
Maybe Job's ancient words need to become painfully modern for us:
בְּרִית כָּרַתִּי לְעֵינָי
“I have made a covenant with my eyes.”
Maybe your covenant with your eyes begins with your screen.
Not because your phone is evil.
Because your heart is valuable.
Because the people on that screen are human beings, not products for your fantasies.
Because your spouse, present or future, deserves covenant faithfulness rather than comparison with an endless feed.
Because your children may someday learn digital holiness by watching you.
Because secret habits eventually shape public character.
Because Christ deserves more than whatever remains of your attention after your appetites have eaten first.
So...
Is following adult creators on social media a form of compromise?

It can be—and when you deliberately follow them in order to feed lust, cultivate sexual fantasy, repeatedly consume sexualized material, or keep yourself near temptation that you know is mastering you, calling it “just following” does not make the underlying desire spiritually neutral.
But do not turn that conclusion into a weapon for policing everybody else's follower list.
Start with your own heart.
Ask yourself before God:
Why am I following?
What am I hoping to see?
What happens inside me when I see it?
Does this lead me toward Christ or repeatedly awaken desires I know I should flee?
Would I defend this behavior because it is genuinely pure—or because I desperately do not want to surrender it?
And perhaps the hardest one:
If Jesus asked for this account tonight, would I give it to Him?
No dramatic music.
No audience.
Just you.
Your phone.
Your history.
Your Savior.
What happens next?
Be honest.

And if Christ has already been freeing you from pornography, lust, sexual compromise, or secret digital habits, tell your testimony. Somebody reading the comments may desperately need evidence that freedom is possible.
Not because every sentence is comfortable.
Not to announce that you are better than anyone.
Not to shame adult creators.
Not to embarrass struggling Christians.

If you genuinely want your online life to glorify God, then let your digital choices become part of your discipleship. Supporting and sharing Christ-centered resources can be one practical way to help truth reach people beyond your own screen—but it should flow from love for Christ, never from guilt, pressure, or an attempt to purchase God's favor.
And do not keep the blessing to yourself.
Invite your family.
Your friends.
The believer who has become lukewarm.
The Christian secretly struggling with lust.
The seeker asking whether Jesus could really forgive them.
Even the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is merely a collection of rules.
But please remember this.
Sharing this article cannot purchase blessing.
Commenting cannot earn forgiveness.
Unfollowing every provocative account on earth cannot wash away one sin.
Jesus does that.
We support Gospel work because we have been loved—not so that we can buy His love.
We share truth because grace found us—not so that sharing can earn grace.
We pursue holiness because Christ saved us—not so holiness can become our Savior.
And maybe that is what somebody needed to hear most.
You are not standing outside Christ's door trying to scrub your search history clean enough to knock.
Come to Him.
Repent.
Believe.
Bring Him the phone.
Bring Him the fantasy.
Bring Him the loneliness underneath it.
Bring Him the marriage you wounded.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the appetite you cannot seem to control.
Bring Him the version of yourself nobody online knows exists.
Bring Him the scandal.
Because the hands that were pierced for sinners are still powerful enough to rewrite what sin tried to make permanent.
And perhaps one day you will look at the account you once thought you could never unfollow...
the habit you thought you could never break...
the shame you thought would follow you into the grave...
and realize Jesus was never trying to take life away from you.
He was calling you back to it.
The screen remembers what you followed—but the cross declares that your past does not get the final word.
